What you'll learn

  • Install Python 3.10 or newer, Git, and VS Code on Windows, macOS, or Linux.
  • Configure Git with your name, email, and main as the default branch.
  • Connect one AI coding assistant: GitHub Copilot Free, or a local model served by Ollama.
  • Create a course virtual environment with jsonschema installed.
  • Run a script that checks every tool and recognize the install problems people hit most.

A coding agent that can edit files and run commands on your laptop is a program running with your permissions. It can delete a folder as easily as you can. So before you hand one a task, you want three things already in place: a language that runs the code it writes, a version-control system that can undo anything it does, and an editor where you can watch every change land.

That is the whole setup for this course. Everything here is free, and no step needs a credit card.

#What each piece does

  • Python 3 runs the practice code and its tests. Most examples use only the standard library. Module 5 adds two packages, jsonschema (installed in Step 5) and the MCP Python SDK (installed in that module).
  • Git takes snapshots of your project. When an agent makes a mess, git diff shows exactly what it touched and git restore puts it back.
  • VS Code is the editor. Its chat panel is where you talk to an assistant, and its source-control view shows every change before you commit it.
  • An AI assistant suggests or makes changes. You pick one in Step 4. The course never depends on a particular company's model; the skills (scoping, reviewing, verifying) transfer to any of them.

#Fixes for the problems people actually hit

⚠️ Watch out

python opens the Microsoft Store, or says it isn't recognized (Windows). Windows ships a placeholder python command. Install the Python install manager from Step 1, then close every terminal and open a new one. In VS Code, also close and reopen the editor so its terminal inherits the new PATH.

⚠️ Watch out

git: command not found right after installing. Same cause: the terminal started before Git existed. Open a new terminal. On macOS, if xcode-select --install says the tools are already installed, git --version should work; if it doesn't, run Software Update and try again.

⚠️ Watch out

Copilot won't activate, or says you don't have access. If your GitHub account gets Copilot through a school or company organization, Copilot Free isn't offered to it, and the organization's settings decide what you can use. Sign out (Accounts menu at the bottom of the Activity Bar) and sign in with a personal account, or use Path B.

⚠️ Watch out

PowerShell says Activate.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system. Windows blocks scripts by default. Allow scripts you create yourself, for your account only, then activate again:

⚠️ Watch out

Ollama says it can't connect, or the model is painfully slow. The ollama command talks to a background server. On Windows and macOS, start the Ollama app; on Linux, run ollama serve in a separate terminal. If answers crawl, your computer is short on memory: try ollama pull qwen3:0.6b, which is about a third of the size, and accept that it will be less accurate.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a practice repository with a module, its tests, a .gitignore, and an AGENTS.md file.
  • Make a checkpoint commit, then give an assistant a small task on its own branch.
  • Read the result with git status, git diff --stat, and git diff, and run the tests yourself.
  • Keep a good change by merging it, or throw a bad one away without losing anything.

Ask an assistant to "add a function" and you may get the function, plus a reformatted file, a renamed variable, and an import you never asked for. None of that is visible in the chat reply. It's only visible if you can compare the project before and after, line by line.

This lesson builds the place where you can always do that: a tiny repository that every later module points agents at. By the end you'll have watched an assistant change it and checked the change yourself.

#What you're building

And this is the workflow you'll repeat all course. The assistant only ever works on a side branch, and main changes only after you've reviewed the work.

#Step 1: Make the folder a repository

In your agent-course folder, open a VS Code terminal and run:

git init creates a hidden .git folder that stores every snapshot. If the code command isn't found (common on macOS), open the folder with File › Open Folder… instead.

#Step 2: Add the code and its tests

Create textstats.py. These are three small functions with clear behavior, so it's easy to tell when a change breaks one.

Look at the last line of output. Three words tie at 2, and top_words lists them alphabetically because the sort key is (-count, word). Tie rules like this are exactly the kind of detail an assistant quietly changes, so the tests pin it down. If an assistant's edit makes any function give the wrong answer, one of these fails. Save this as test_textstats.py in the same folder:

Run the whole suite from the terminal (python3 on macOS and Linux):

python -m unittest finds every file whose name starts with test and runs each method whose name starts with test. Five methods, five ok lines. Memorize the shape of this output, because "Ran 5 tests ... OK" is the evidence you'll ask agents for in Module 4.

#Step 3: Tell people and agents how the project works

README.md is for humans. Two lines are enough:

AGENTS.md is a plain Markdown file of instructions for coding agents. It's an open convention, and many agent tools, VS Code's included, read it automatically from the repository root. Keep it short and specific:

Finally .gitignore, which lists files Git should never track. A .env file is where secret keys usually live, so it goes first:

#Step 4: Make a checkpoint commit

Your hash will be different. This commit is the snapshot you can always return to, no matter what happens next.

#Step 5: Give the assistant a small task on a branch

Create the branch first, so the assistant's changes never land on main:

Open the Chat view, choose the mode or agent that can edit files, and paste this task:

If your assistant asks permission to edit a file or run the test command, read what it wants to do and allow it. Don't approve anything you don't recognize. No assistant working yet? Make the change by hand; the review steps below work the same.

#Step 6: Review what actually changed

Start with the summary views:

Two files, both named in the task. That's the first thing to check every time: is the list of touched files the list you expected? A third file here, say a rewritten README.md, would be a reason to slow down. Then read the change itself with git diff textstats.py:

Lines starting with + were added; there are no - lines, so nothing old was removed. The strict > is what makes ties return the first word: a later word of equal length never replaces it. Your assistant's version may look different and still be correct.

Now run the tests yourself, even if the assistant pasted output. You should see Ran 7 tests and OK. One more thing to notice: longest_word("Hello, world") returns "Hello," with the comma. Is that right? The task never said, so that gap is the task writer's, not the assistant's. Module 2 is about writing tasks without gaps like that.

💡 Tip

In VS Code, the Source Control view (the branch icon in the Activity Bar) shows the same diff side by side. Click a file there to compare old and new versions.

#Step 7: Keep it or throw it away

If you're happy, commit on the branch and merge into main:

If you're not, discard the edits and delete the branch:

git restore . puts every tracked file back to the last commit. If the assistant also created new files, git clean -n lists them, and git clean -f deletes them, so always run the -n preview first.

⚠️ Watch out

Uncommitted changes don't stay behind on a branch. If you run git switch main before you commit or restore, the edited files come with you to main. Commit or restore first, then switch.

🧪 Try it yourself

Before moving on, run git log --oneline --graph --all. If you merged, both commits now sit on main. Because main hadn't moved since you branched, Git simply slid main forward to the branch's commit (a fast-forward) instead of making a separate merge commit. If you threw the change away, you'll see only the checkpoint.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Follow five safety rules for every assistant or agent session in this course.
  • Scan text for secrets before pasting it, and know what to do if one leaks anyway.
  • Undo any agent change with the right Git command, from one file to a whole branch.
  • Recognize a stuck agent, stop it, and restart with a smaller task.
  • Turn on the accessibility and privacy settings you need.

You paste an error message into a chat to ask why your script can't reach its database. The assistant answers helpfully. Then you notice the third line of what you pasted: postgres://admin:hunter2@db.example.com/shop. The password is now in a chat log on a server you don't control, and deleting the message doesn't un-send it.

The only real fix is to change the password (and for API keys, to revoke the key and make a new one). That takes five minutes if you notice and a bad week if you don't. Most of this lesson is about never needing it.

#Five rules for every session

These hold for the rest of the course, and they're a sensible baseline for real work too.

  1. Secrets never go into a prompt. No API keys, tokens, passwords, .env contents, or private keys, and no screenshots of them. Agents shouldn't read files that hold them either, which is why AGENTS.md says so and .gitignore lists .env.
  2. Every task starts from a clean commit on its own branch. Run git status first. If it isn't clean, commit or stash before the agent starts, so its changes are the only changes.
  3. You read every diff before it's committed. The agent's summary describes what it meant to do. The diff shows what it did.
  4. You approve only commands you can explain. If an agent asks to run something like rm -rf build/ && pip install -U ..., you should be able to say what each part does before clicking allow.
  5. Practice folders hold practice data. No school files, personal photos, or real customer data in any folder an agent can open.

#Scan before you paste

Secrets have recognizable shapes. GitHub personal access tokens start with ghp_ or github_pat_, AWS access key IDs start with AKIA, and private key files start with a -----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY----- line. A few regular expressions catch most of them:

Two hits, and the redacted version still has everything the assistant needs to explain a timeout. The (?<=://) and (?=@) parts are lookarounds: they require :// before the match and @ after it without including them, so only admin:hunter2 gets replaced.

Notice what the scanner didn't flag on line 5. The key=value pattern wants token as a whole word, and in GITHUB_TOKEN the underscore glues it to GITHUB. The ghp_ rule caught it instead. Pattern scanners always miss something, so treat this as a seatbelt, not a guarantee: you still read what you paste.

🧪 Try it yourself

Add a line "api_key = " + "abc123" to report and run it again. Which pattern fires? Then change it to "apikey: abc123". Does the scanner still catch it, and why?

#If a secret leaks anyway

Order matters. First revoke or rotate it on the service that issued it (GitHub: Settings › Developer settings › Personal access tokens), because anything already copied stays valid until you do. Only then clean up the chat, the file, or the commit. If it reached a Git commit, deleting the file in a new commit doesn't remove it from history; GitHub's guide on removing sensitive data, linked below, explains why rewriting history is a last resort and rotation comes first.

GitHub's push protection can also block many known token formats when you push to a GitHub repository, but it only recognizes the formats it was built to find. Your own habits are the main defense.

#Undo anything with Git

Every agent run in this course starts from a commit, so every mistake has an exact way back:

Situation Command
See what changed git status, then git diff
Throw away edits to one file git restore textstats.py
Throw away all edits to tracked files git restore .
List new files the agent created git clean -n (preview only)
Delete those new files git clean -f (after checking the preview)
Set work aside to try something else git stash, later git stash pop
Undo the last commit but keep its edits git reset --soft HEAD~1
Abandon a whole branch git switch main, then git branch -D ai/name

git restore and git clean -f can't be undone themselves, because the discarded edits were never committed. That's fine for agent output you've decided to reject. It's another reason to commit your own work before every session.

#When an agent gets stuck

Agents get stuck in recognizable ways: they run the same failing command again and again, their diff keeps growing, they start editing the tests so the tests pass, or they apologize and redo the same change. Don't keep typing "try again." Each retry fills the conversation with failed attempts that the model then reads as context.

Stopping a request ends the loop, but it doesn't undo edits already made, so the Git step always comes next. Starting a new chat matters too: a fresh session isn't anchored to the earlier wrong turns.

#Keep a session log

Make a notes folder next to practice-repo (outside it, so agents working in the repo don't read your notes) and keep one file per module. After each session, write five lines:

The last line is the one that makes you better at this. Over a few weeks it becomes your personal list of what to put in every task.

#Accessibility and privacy settings

VS Code has solid accessibility support, and the chat works with it:

  • Zoom the whole editor with Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- (Cmd+= and Cmd+- on a Mac).
  • High contrast: press Ctrl+K Ctrl+T (Cmd+K Cmd+T on a Mac) to open the color theme picker, then choose a High Contrast theme.
  • Screen readers: run Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode from the Command Palette. Accessible View (Alt+F2 on Windows, Option+F2 on macOS, Shift+Alt+F2 on Linux) lets you read a chat response line by line.

On privacy: with Copilot, your prompts and the code it reads are sent to GitHub's servers. The free plan has telemetry turned on by default; setting telemetry.telemetryLevel to off in VS Code's settings turns VS Code's telemetry off. With Ollama, the model runs on your machine and prompts stay there.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You realize an API key was in text you pasted into a chat ten minutes ago. What do you do first?

  • The text was already sent and may be stored; deleting the message doesn't make the key unusable.

  • Once the old key stops working, a copy of it is harmless. Clean up the chat afterward.

  • That stops future commits of the file, but the key in the chat is still valid.

Show answer

B. Once the old key stops working, a copy of it is harmless. Clean up the chat afterward.

2An agent has edited six files and is now changing test_textstats.py to make a test pass. What's the best next move?

  • Retrying in the same conversation keeps the failed attempts in its context; it often repeats them.

  • Committing locks in changes you haven't reviewed, including the edited test.

  • Git gets you back to the checkpoint, and a smaller task in a fresh session is far more likely to succeed.

Show answer

C. Git gets you back to the checkpoint, and a smaller task in a fresh session is far more likely to succeed.

3Why does the session log live in notes/ beside the repo instead of inside it?

  • Git tracks text files well; that isn't the reason.

  • Keeping notes outside the folder you hand to an agent is the same idea as keeping secrets out of it.

Show answer

B. Keeping notes outside the folder you hand to an agent is the same idea as keeping secrets out of it.

#Further reading

  • Removing sensitive data from a repository (opens in a new tab): GitHub's guide, including why you rotate the secret before rewriting history.
  • Secure AI-assisted development in VS Code (opens in a new tab): trust boundaries, approvals for tool calls and terminal commands, and sandboxing.
  • gitignore (opens in a new tab): the full pattern rules, including how to ignore a folder but keep one file in it.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compare autocomplete, chat, and agents by what each can see, what it can change, and how you review it.
  • Explain the agent loop (model, tool call, result, model) and where it stops.
  • Sort engineering tasks into good and bad candidates for delegation.
  • Write a task spec with scope, acceptance criteria, and a stop-and-ask rule.

Type "improve the app" into an agent that can edit files and run commands, then go get a snack. When you come back there are 31 changed files, a new dependency, a renamed database column, and a cheerful summary. Was any of it wrong? You can't say, because the request never defined what "improved" means, which files were fair game, or when to stop.

An agent will always do something with a vague request. The fix isn't a smarter model. It's a better task.

#Three tools that act at three different scales

All three are the same kind of model underneath. What differs is how much of your project they can see and how much they can change before you look.

Autocomplete Chat Agent
What it sees Code around your cursor What you paste or attach Whatever its tools can reach
What it changes Nothing until you press Tab Nothing until you apply a suggestion Files and commands, by itself, in a loop
Size of one step A line or a block An answer or a snippet A multi-file change
How you review Read it before accepting Read it before applying Read the diff and rerun the checks

Use autocomplete when you know what you're writing and want it typed faster, chat for questions and small snippets you'll read before pasting, and an agent when the work needs dependent steps: read these files, change them, run the tests, fix what broke.

Each step up the table saves more typing and removes one more moment where you'd naturally notice a mistake. That trade is the subject of this whole course.

#What actually makes something an agent

Here's the intuition. A language model only produces text. It can't open a file. What it can do is write a structured request ("call read_file with path='textstats.py'"). A program wrapped around the model, called the harness, reads that request, runs the real function, and sends the result back as the next message. The model reads the result and decides what to request next.

Now precisely: an agent is a loop in which a model chooses actions, a harness executes them as tool calls, and each result is appended to the conversation before the model is called again. The loop ends when the model replies with no tool call, or when the harness stops it.

You can see the mechanics without any real model. This ScriptedModel returns pre-written replies in order, the way a test double stands in for a real service. Everything else is exactly what a harness does.

Three things to notice. One question cost three model calls, because every tool result goes back to the model; that's why agents are slower and pricier than chat. The line TOOLS[reply["tool"]](**reply["args"]) is the only place anything happens, and it belongs to the harness, so the harness is where limits and permissions belong. And for ... else gives the loop a ceiling: if the model never stops asking, MAX_STEPS stops it.

A real harness differs in one place: respond sends messages to a model and parses the tool call out of its reply. Module 5 covers how real tool calls are described and validated.

#Watching the loop handle a missing file

Step through this smaller loop. Watch context grow and look at what happens on the second tool call, which asks for a file that doesn't exist.

The missing file doesn't crash anything. The harness returns "error: not found" as an ordinary result, and a real model would read it and adjust, perhaps by listing files first. Returning errors as results is what lets an agent recover from its own wrong guesses.

#The loop stops, but "done" isn't proof

An agent loop ends in one of four ways: the model sends a reply without a tool call, the harness hits a step or cost limit, a tool fails in a way the harness treats as fatal, or a human presses stop. Only the first looks like success, and it's just the model's claim. A model can answer "Done, all tests pass" without ever having run them.

So a good task says, in advance, what evidence will count as done. You'll check that evidence yourself (Module 4), and in the next lesson you'll build a harness that checks it automatically.

#What to delegate, and what not to

A task is a good fit for an agent when it is bounded (you can name the files), checkable (a command can show it worked), and reversible (a branch and git restore undo it).

Task Delegate to an agent? Why
Add tests for top_words covering ties and punctuation Yes Small scope, and the tests themselves are the evidence
Rename char_count to count_chars everywhere in the repo Yes Mechanical; search and the test suite confirm it
Fix the failing test in test_textstats.py (error output attached) Yes The cause is visible and the test defines done
Improve the app No No boundary, no acceptance test, no stopping point
Rotate the production database password No Needs secrets and can't be undone with Git
Decide whether we should switch web frameworks Not as an edit task A judgment call; ask for a written comparison, then decide yourself
Change one string literal No (just do it) Faster to type than to describe and review

#Anatomy of a task spec

Here's the punctuation gap from the previous module's longest_word, written as a task an agent can't misread:

Every section answers a question the agent would otherwise guess at. Context saves it from rediscovering what you already know. Scope and out of scope give it a boundary. Acceptance criteria are things a command can check, so "done" has a meaning. Stop and ask turns the risky moments into a pause instead of a guess. Report tells it what evidence to bring back.

Look at criterion 1 closely. "Hello" and "world" are both five letters once the punctuation is gone, so this one example checks the stripping and the tie rule.

⚠️ Watch out

Criteria a command can't check. "The code should be clean and efficient" gives the agent nothing to aim at and you nothing to verify. Replace it with something testable: "runs top_words on a 10,000-word text in under 0.1 s," or "no function longer than 30 lines."

⚠️ Watch out

Handing over the whole repo when two files matter. An agent with no scope reads widely and edits widely. Name the files. If you don't know which files are involved, that's a separate, read-only task: ask it to find them first.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In agent_loop.py, why did one question lead to three calls to the model?

  • No error occurred; both tool calls succeeded.

  • Two tool calls plus the final answer means three model calls. More tools, more calls.

  • MAX_STEPS is a ceiling, not a minimum; the loop broke out at step 3 on its own.

Show answer

B. Two tool calls plus the final answer means three model calls. More tools, more calls.

2Where is the right place to enforce "the agent may not delete files"?

  • A prompt is a request. The model can misread it, ignore it, or be talked out of it.

  • The model can only ask. If the harness never runs a delete, no reply can cause one.

  • You don't control training, and no training guarantees behavior on every input.

Show answer

B. The model can only ask. If the harness never runs a delete, no reply can cause one.

3Which acceptance criterion could a reviewer actually check?

  • Which edge cases? "Properly" by whose standard? Nothing here can pass or fail.

  • This is an opinion, not a check.

  • One input, one exact expected output. A test can confirm or refute it in milliseconds.

Show answer

C. One input, one exact expected output. A test can confirm or refute it in milliseconds.

Key takeaways

  • Autocomplete, chat, and agents differ in how much they can see and change before you review.
  • An agent is a loop: the model requests a tool, the harness runs it, the result goes back to the model.
  • Only the harness acts, so limits and permissions belong in the harness, not the prompt.
  • A loop ending with "done" is a claim; the task should say what evidence proves it.
  • A good task spec states the goal, context, scope, checkable acceptance criteria, when to stop and ask, and what to report.

#Further reading

  • Building effective agents (opens in a new tab): an essay from Anthropic's engineers, with advice that applies to any model: start with the simplest workflow that works and add autonomy only when it pays off.
  • Agents in VS Code (opens in a new tab): how the editor's agent sessions use tools, and where approvals fit.

What you'll learn

  • Build a tool registry whose write_file tool refuses paths outside the task's scope.
  • Run the model-tool-result loop with a hard step limit.
  • Check acceptance criteria in the harness itself, independent of what the model claims.
  • See how a careful, a corner-cutting, and a looping model each end up.

In the previous lesson the loop answered a question. This time it changes code, which raises the stakes. The model will say it's done; the harness is going to find out for itself.

You'll build mini_harness.py: a harness that gives a model four tools over a tiny in-memory repo, enforces which files it may write, stops it after a fixed number of steps, and then runs the tests itself to decide the verdict. Instead of a real model, three ScriptedModels play three characters you'll meet in real agent work.

#Step 1: A repo the harness can test

The repo is a dictionary from file name to source code. apply_discount has a bug: it divides by 10 where it should divide by 100. One of the two tests catches it.

run_tests loads each non-test file as a module, loads the test files, and runs them with unittest. It returns counts instead of raising, because a tool that crashes takes the whole harness down with it.

Two tests ran and one failed: 2000 - 2000 * 10 // 10 is 0, not 1800. Registering the module in sys.modules is what lets the test file's from pricing import apply_discount find it.

#Step 2: Tools that enforce the task's scope

A Workspace holds a copy of the files and the four tools. The important line is the first one in write_file: a path outside allowed_writes gets a refusal as a result, so the model learns it was blocked and the loop keeps going.

All three probes return strings. The model can't tell a refusal from any other result except by reading it, and that's fine: what matters is that the test file was never touched. dict(files) matters too. Without the copy, every workspace would share and edit the same START dictionary.

#Step 3: A scripted model and the loop

The ScriptedModel plays back replies and ignores the conversation, which makes every run identical. describe shortens arguments for printing, so a file's full contents show up as <173 chars>.

The loop is the one from the Notes lesson with two upgrades: unknown tools return an error result, and every action is printed, giving you a transcript to review afterward.

This is what good agent behavior looks like: look around, read the code, reproduce the failure before changing anything, make one edit, and rerun the tests. Step 3 matters more than it seems. A test that was already failing before your change tells you something different from one that started failing after it.

#Step 4: The finish line

The careful model says the tests pass. The transcript agrees. The harness checks anyway, because a transcript is just more text, and a different model could write the same sentence with no test run behind it.

finish_line reruns the tests on the workspace's final files, requires at least as many tests as at the start (so deleting tests can't count as passing), and lists every file that differs from START.

Even a PASS ends at "ready for human review," not "merged." The harness has checked what a machine can check. Whether // 100 is the right fix for the business (should the discount round down or to the nearest cent?) is still your call.

#Step 5: A model that cuts corners

This model doesn't fix the bug. It tries to change the test's expected value to match the broken output, then claims success.

The write was denied, so nothing changed, and the finish line catches the false claim: same failing test as at the start. Two separate defenses did two separate jobs here. Scope enforcement stopped the bad edit. The finish line stopped the bad claim.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change allowed_writes to {"pricing.py", "test_pricing.py"} in this cell and run it again. The harness check now says PASS, because the weakened test agrees with the broken code. Look at files changed: that line is the only clue. Scope rules and diff review exist for exactly this case.

#Step 6: A model that never stops

Some models get stuck rerunning the same command. max_steps is the backstop:

Without the limit, a real loop like this keeps calling a paid model until someone notices. With it, the run ends after three steps with no answer and an honest FAIL.

#The finished harness

Here is the whole program in one file. It runs all three models in turn.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does finish_line rerun the tests instead of reading the last run_tests result from the transcript?

  • It's slower, if anything. Speed isn't the reason.

  • A model could stop before its last test run, edit after it, or simply claim a result. Only a fresh check of the final state counts.

  • They don't. The point is independence from the model, not freshness.

Show answer

B. A model could stop before its last test run, edit after it, or simply claim a result. Only a fresh check of the final state counts.

2What does outcome["ran"] >= BASELINE protect against?

  • The number of runs doesn't matter; this compares how many tests exist.

  • Zero failures out of zero tests isn't success. Requiring the original test count closes that gap.

  • Nothing here measures time.

Show answer

B. Zero failures out of zero tests isn't success. Requiring the original test count closes that gap.

3In the try above, the sneaky model passed once it was allowed to write the test file. Which part of the harness still revealed the problem?

  • The sneaky model finished in three steps, well under the limit.

  • PASS was the misleading part: the weakened test agreed with the broken code.

  • A bug fix that only touches the test file is a red flag a reviewer spots in seconds.

Show answer

C. A bug fix that only touches the test file is a red flag a reviewer spots in seconds.

Key takeaways

  • Every tool returns a string, including refusals and errors, so the loop never crashes on a bad request.
  • Scope is enforced where the tool runs (write_file), not in the task text.
  • max_steps turns a stuck model into a clean failure instead of an endless bill.
  • The finish line reruns the acceptance check on the final files and ignores the model's claim.
  • A PASS means "ready for human review," and the list of changed files is the first thing that review reads.

#Ideas to extend it

  • When the finish line fails, append its result to messages and give the model one more chance, then stop for good.
  • Add a max_writes limit, so a model can't rewrite the same file twenty times.
  • Save the transcript to transcript.json with json.dump, so you can review a run after the fact.
  • Swap ScriptedModel for a local model through Ollama's tool-calling API (linked below). The rest of the harness doesn't change.

#Further reading

  • Ollama tool calling (opens in a new tab): the real message format for tool requests and tool results, which maps onto messages here.
  • unittest (opens in a new tab): TestLoader, TestSuite, and TextTestRunner, the three pieces run_tests is built from.

What you'll learn

  • Match requests to autocomplete, chat, an agent, or doing it yourself.
  • Rewrite a vague request as a spec and find the holes in someone else's.
  • Write a linter that flags missing sections and uncheckable acceptance criteria.
  • Harden a loop against bad tool calls, repeated actions, and oversized results, and add one retry with feedback.

The first three exercises are about the words you hand an agent; the last three and the challenge are about the code wrapped around it. Every code solution is plain Python with a scripted model, so you can run it offline.

#Warm-up: pick the right tool

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You're writing a loop and know exactly what the next three lines should be.

  • You already know the answer; you just want it typed. Accept with Tab, reading it as you do.

  • Spinning up a multi-step loop for three lines you could type is slower and harder to review.

  • Chat works, but copying an answer back is slower than an inline suggestion.

Show answer

A. You already know the answer; you just want it typed. Accept with Tab, reading it as you do.

2A test fails with KeyError: 'total' and you don't understand the traceback.

  • You don't know the cause yet, so you can't write acceptance criteria for a fix.

  • You need an explanation first. Once you understand the bug, you can decide whether to fix it yourself or delegate.

  • Autocomplete continues code; it doesn't explain errors.

Show answer

B. You need an explanation first. Once you understand the bug, you can decide whether to fix it yourself or delegate.

3Rename char_count to count_chars in four files and update every call and test.

  • Possible, but it's mechanical, multi-file, and easy to verify, which is the sweet spot for an agent.

  • Bounded, checkable with two commands, and reversible.

  • Chat would hand you edits to paste into four files yourself.

Show answer

B. Bounded, checkable with two commands, and reversible.

4Decide whether the project should move from unittest to pytest.

  • A tooling decision has trade-offs only you and your team can weigh. Letting an agent decide by doing it skips the decision.

  • The model can lay out trade-offs; the choice and its consequences stay with you.

Show answer

B. The model can lay out trade-offs; the choice and its consequences stay with you.

#Exercise 1: Turn a complaint into a spec

A teammate sends: "top_words is weird with some inputs, can you get the AI to fix it?" You investigate and find:

A negative n slices from the end (ranked[:-1]) and silently drops the last word. Write a complete task spec for an agent, using the sections from the Notes lesson: goal, context, in scope, out of scope, acceptance criteria, stop and ask if, report.

Need a hint?

Decide the behavior before you write the spec. Should n=-1 raise an error, return [], or return everything? An agent will pick one if you don't. Then make each acceptance criterion a single input with an exact expected result.

Show solution

One good spec (yours may choose different behavior, as long as it states it):

Criterion 2 matters: it pins down the edge next to the bug, so the fix can't accidentally break n=0. The "stop and ask" line covers the one thing that would make the fix wrong, which is code that relies on the old behavior.

#Exercise 2: Find the holes in this spec

List at least four problems, and say what an agent might do because of each one.

Need a hint?

Go section by section: which of the usual sections are missing? Then, for each criterion, ask "what command would show this passed?"

Show solution
  • No scope. The agent may "clean up" the tests too, or add new files. Name the functions and files.
  • No out of scope. Nothing stops it from renaming public functions, which breaks every caller.
  • Criterion 1 can't be checked. "Cleaner" is a matter of taste; the agent decides alone what it means.
  • Criterion 2 can be gamed. Tests can pass because tests were deleted, skipped, or loosened. Say "with no test removed, skipped, or edited."
  • Criterion 3 can't be checked. No number and no benchmark.
  • No stop condition and no report. The agent never pauses, and you get a summary instead of evidence.

The deeper problem: "clean up" isn't a task, it's a mood. Rewrite it as one concrete change (for example, "replace the manual counting dict in top_words with collections.Counter, no behavior change"), and most of these holes close on their own.

#Exercise 3: A spec linter

Write lint_spec(text) that returns a list of problems. It should report each missing section heading (Goal:, In scope:, Out of scope:, Acceptance criteria:, Stop and ask if:) and each acceptance criterion that uses a vague word (clean, better, properly, fast, and so on) without any number in it. Sample output for the spec in the solution:

Need a hint?

Walk the lines with a flag that turns on after Acceptance criteria: and off at the next line that looks like a heading. Strip the list number (1.) before checking for digits, or every numbered criterion will look measurable.

Show solution

Criterion 3 passes the linter because "10000 words" gives it something to measure. A linter like this can't judge whether a criterion is good, only whether it's the kind of sentence that could possibly be checked. That's still enough to catch the most common mistake.

#Exercise 4: Turn every tool failure into a result

This line from the harness is a crash waiting to happen on three kinds of bad request: an unknown tool name, wrong argument names, and a tool that raises.

Write call_tool(name, args) that always returns a string. Error messages should help the model fix its next request (for example, by listing the tools that do exist).

Need a hint?

Check the name before calling. Then wrap the call in try, catching TypeError (raised when keyword arguments don't match the function) separately from everything else.

Show solution

One caution: catching TypeError around the call also catches a TypeError raised inside the tool, which would get the misleading "bad arguments" label. Module 5 fixes this properly by validating arguments against a schema before the call.

#Exercise 5: Stop a model that repeats itself

Add stuck detection to a loop: if the model makes the exact same tool call (same name and same arguments) three times in a row, stop with a message. A model that alternates between different calls should not be stopped.

Need a hint?

Turn each call into something hashable, like (name, tuple(sorted(args.items()))), keep the last three in a list, and stop when the list is full and len(set(recent)) == 1.

Show solution

The stuck model is stopped at step 4, long before the 10-step limit, which saves six model calls. The varied model calls run_tests twice but not in a row, so it's left alone. Repeating a test run after an edit is normal; repeating it with nothing changed in between is the sign of a stuck loop.

#Exercise 6: Keep huge tool results from flooding the context

A test run over 300 tests prints thousands of characters, and every one of them goes back to the model on every later step. Write clip(result, limit=120) that returns short results unchanged and shortens long ones, keeping the start and the end with a marker in between that says how much was cut.

Need a hint?

The end of a test log is where the summary lives (FAILED (failures=1)). Keep limit // 2 characters from each end.

Show solution

If you kept only the first 120 characters, the model would see a wall of ok lines and never learn that a test failed. The marker matters as well: it tells the model (and you, reading the transcript) that something was left out, so neither of you mistakes the clipped text for the whole output.

#Challenge: One retry with feedback, then stop

Write run_with_one_retry(model, task). It runs the agent loop; if the acceptance check fails, it appends a user message describing the failure and runs the loop once more on the same conversation. If the check still fails, it gives up and says a human should take over. Use a scripted model whose first fix is wrong and whose second is right.

Need a hint?

Keep messages outside the inner loop so the second attempt can see the first attempt's tool results and your feedback. Make the acceptance check run real code (exec the file and call the function) rather than searching the source for a string.

Show solution

The first "fix" gives 2000 - 20 = 1980, so the check fails and the model gets one concrete sentence of feedback. Why only one retry? Each extra attempt costs model calls and adds more failed work to the context, and after two misses the problem is usually the task or the model, not bad luck. A human looking at it fresh is cheaper.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Ask an AI for a read-only map of a repository, with a file and line for every claim.
  • Sort the map's claims by how hard they are to verify, and check them with git ls-files, git grep, and the test suite.
  • Review an agent's plan for grounding, scope, order, verification, risky steps, and hidden assumptions.
  • Rewrite a bad plan into one you'd approve.

The task was one sentence: "late_fee charges 25 cents when a book comes back on time; fix it." The agent's reply opened with a plan:

It hasn't opened the file with the bug. It hasn't read the repository's instructions, which forbid touching migrations/. It has no step that runs a test. And it reads confidently enough that a tired reviewer might type "sounds good." This module is about the two habits that stop that: verify what the agent says about the code, and read its plan like a reviewer before a single file changes.

#Start with what the repository says about itself

Most repositories explain themselves, if anyone reads them. Before trusting any map, human or AI, look at:

  • README.md for what the project is and how to run it.
  • AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, or similar for rules: test commands, style, off-limits folders.
  • Dependency files (requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, package.json) for the real stack.
  • Entry points and routes, where requests or commands come in.
  • Tests, both for how to run them and for what behavior someone cared enough to pin down.
  • CI configuration (.github/workflows/) for the checks that run on every push.

Then give the AI a read-only mapping task. Saying "read-only" up front means a mapping question can't turn into an edit:

#A map is a list of claims

Whatever comes back, treat each sentence as a claim to check, not a fact. Claims come in kinds, and they don't cost the same to verify:

Kind of claim Example How hard to verify
Something exists "Routes are in app/routes.py" Easy: list the files
Something is defined somewhere "late_fee is in app/pricing.py" Easy: one search
Behavior "late_fee caps the fee at 500" Medium: read the code or run it
Absence "Nothing calls late_fee outside the tests" Hard: you have to search everywhere, and dynamic calls can hide

Absence claims are where AI maps go wrong most often. A model that read three files and didn't see a call will happily report "it's never called," because from where it stood that looked true.

#Check claims with search and with tests

Here's the bookshelf repository from the hook, built from plain strings so you can run it anywhere. Save and run it locally if you want to try the Git commands below on a real folder.

In a real repository, git ls-files prints that same list: every file Git tracks, which skips ignored clutter like __pycache__/. And git grep -n searches only those files, with line numbers:

Suppose the AI's map said four things. This script checks each one against the files, with a small grep that works like git grep -n, and prints its evidence:

Two of four claims are false, and they're false in instructive ways. The SQLite claim is half right: the database is real, but app/db.py doesn't exist. That's the most common shape of an AI mistake, the right idea at a plausible but wrong path. The "only called from tests" claim misses routes.py:17, the line customers actually hit. An agent that believed it might "fix" late_fee in a way that only the test exercises.

The last claim is true, and it's the most useful one: no test covers the on-time case, which is exactly why the bug survived. The fix should start by adding that test.

💡 Tip

Searches find text, not meaning. late_fee could also be reached through getattr(module, "late_" + "fee"), a template, or a config file. A search with no hits is strong evidence of absence in a small Python repo and weaker evidence in a large one.

#Read the plan like a reviewer

Now go back to the plan from the hook and put it through six questions:

Question What to look for The bookshelf plan
Grounded? Does each step name files that exist, and did the agent read them? Never mentions app/pricing.py, the file with the bug
Scoped? Does every step serve the task? Steps 1–5 are a rewrite; none of them fixes late_fee
Ordered? Read, reproduce, change, verify, in that order? No reading, no reproducing the bug
Verified? Is there a step with a named test command? The last step is "Done"
Risky steps? Deletes, schema or dependency changes, anything Git can't undo? Deletes migrations/ (forbidden by AGENTS.md) and swaps the database
Assumptions? What must be true for this to work? That you want a rewrite, and that live data can move to PostgreSQL

A plan that fails "grounded" usually fails everything else, because a plan written before reading the code is a plan for some other repository. Here's one you'd approve:

Step 4 is the one to look for in every bug-fix plan: a test that fails before the change. If the new test passes before you've fixed anything, it isn't testing the bug.

⚠️ Watch out

Trusting "I've reviewed the codebase." That sentence doesn't say which files were read. Ask for the list, and compare it with git ls-files. Agents often read only the first part of long files, so ask about line ranges, too.

⚠️ Watch out

Approving a plan because each step sounds reasonable. "Update requirements.txt" is a fine step in general. Check each step against this task. A step that doesn't move the task forward is scope creep, however sensible it sounds.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1An AI's map says "format_date is unused; it's safe to delete." What should you do before believing it?

  • You don't know what it searched. An absence claim is the hardest kind to trust.

  • A search over every tracked file is the minimum. Indirect references are why "no hits" is evidence, not proof.

  • Starting proves very little; the caller might run only on one rarely used page.

Show answer

B. A search over every tracked file is the minimum. Indirect references are why "no hits" is evidence, not proof.

2In check_claims.py, why is the SQLite claim marked FALSE even though the app really uses SQLite?

  • The regex found three matches, all in app/storage.py.

  • The idea was right and the location was invented. An agent acting on it would edit or create the wrong file.

  • It's a real, widely used database; that's not the issue.

Show answer

B. The idea was right and the location was invented. An agent acting on it would edit or create the wrong file.

3Which step most clearly shows a plan was written before reading the code?

  • A grounded plan starts from the code involved. Missing it means the plan came from general knowledge, not this repo.

  • That's out of scope here, but plans written after reading can also over-reach.

  • Length says nothing about grounding.

Show answer

A. A grounded plan starts from the code involved. Missing it means the plan came from general knowledge, not this repo.

Key takeaways

  • Read README.md, AGENTS.md, dependency files, entry points, and tests before trusting any map of a repo.
  • Ask for maps read-only, with file:line for each claim and inferences marked.
  • Check claims with git ls-files, git grep -n, and the tests; absence claims need the most care.
  • A plan passes review when it's grounded, scoped, ordered, verified, honest about risky steps, and explicit about assumptions.
  • A good bug-fix plan adds a test that fails before the change.

#Further reading

  • git grep (opens in a new tab): flags worth knowing are -n (line numbers), -w (whole words), and -e (several patterns).
  • AGENTS.md (opens in a new tab): the open format for repository instructions aimed at coding agents, with examples of what to put in one.
  • git ls-files (opens in a new tab): list tracked files, or with --others --exclude-standard, untracked ones an agent may have created.

What you'll learn

  • Ask a model for a plan as structured JSON and handle replies that aren't.
  • Check each step against the repository's real file list to catch invented paths.
  • Enforce the task's scope and the repository's protected folders.
  • Flag edits made before reading, plans with no final test run, and steps that need a human's approval.

Reading a plan carefully works, but it's slow, and the mistakes in the previous lesson were mechanical: a file that doesn't exist, an edit outside scope, a forbidden folder, no test step. Mechanical mistakes are what code is for. You'll build plan_check.py, a reviewer that catches them in milliseconds so your own attention goes to the questions code can't answer.

Here's the end result. Given the "modernize" plan from the Notes lesson, the checker prints this (the full program at the bottom produces it):

#Step 1: The repo and its real file list

The checker needs the truth to compare against. In a real repository that's git ls-files, which you'd call from Python like this:

Here, so everything runs without Git, tracked_files walks a folder and skips what Git would skip. The repository is the bookshelf app, trimmed to one line per file because only the names matter today.

as_posix() matters on Windows, where paths use backslashes. Without it, app\pricing.py would never match the app/pricing.py in a plan.

#Step 2: Ask for the plan as data

You can't check a paragraph with code. So the prompt asks for a fixed shape, which most models (local ones included) follow when you're this specific:

Models don't always comply, so parsing has to handle a reply that isn't JSON. The scripted model below returns the "modernize" plan first, then a chatty prose reply, to test both paths.

The first reply parses into six steps. The second fails cleanly with a reason you could send straight back to the model. Notice isinstance(plan, dict): a reply of [1, 2] is valid JSON too, and without that guard plan.get would crash.

#Step 3: Is every step grounded in real files?

Reading, editing, or deleting a file that doesn't exist means the plan was written from imagination. Creating a file that already exists means it would be overwritten. Both are hard stops, so they get the severity BLOCK.

One hit: app/models.py is invented. Every other path in this bad plan is real, which is a useful reminder that grounding alone doesn't make a plan good.

#Step 4: Does every change stay inside the task?

The task allows two files. AGENTS.md protects migrations/. fnmatch handles patterns like migrations/*, so the scope can be a list of globs instead of exact names.

Every change in the plan is out of bounds, and none of them touches app/pricing.py. Protected paths are checked first, so the migration gets the more specific message.

#Step 5: Does the plan read before it edits?

An edit to a file the agent hasn't read is a guess about what's in it. That's worth fixing but not always fatal (an agent may have read the file in an earlier session), so it's a WARN.

#Step 6: Does a test run come after the last change?

A plan whose last step is an edit ends with an unverified claim. The check finds the last change and looks for a test command after it.

"After the last change" is the important part. A test run in the middle of a plan proves the code worked at that moment, before the remaining edits.

#Step 7: Flag steps a human must approve

Some steps can be correct and still need a person to say yes. Deletions get flagged, because a file Git can restore may still have had effects outside the repo (a migration that already ran against a real database, say). Dependency files get flagged, because they change what every install downloads. These are ASK findings.

#Step 8: One verdict

check_plan runs all five checks, sorts the findings by step so they read in order, and turns the worst severity into a verdict. Then it runs on the modernize plan and on the focused plan from the Notes lesson.

Thirteen findings against zero. A checker this simple can't tell you the focused plan's fix is right. It tells you the plan is shaped like a plan you could review, which is what you want from code before a human spends attention on it.

🧪 Try it yourself

Delete the last step (the final run) from FOCUSED and run the cell again. Which check fires, and on which step number? Then move the read app/pricing.py step to the end. What changes?

#The finished checker

The finished version folds the five checks into one pass over the steps. steps[changes[-1]:] is the slice after the last change, because step numbers start at 1 while list indexes start at 0.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Why is "edit before reading" a WARN while "read a file that doesn't exist" is a BLOCK?

  • The agent may know the file from earlier work, but no plan can be right about a file that isn't there.

  • All findings are computed at once; severity is about what each one proves.

  • Reading is how an agent learns the code. It's flagged because skipping it is risky.

Show answer

A. The agent may know the file from earlier work, but no plan can be right about a file that isn't there.

2The scope check compares paths against task["allowed"]. Why not just trust the plan's why fields?

  • They're often filled in, and they can sound perfectly reasonable.

  • "Swap flask for fastapi" explains the step but doesn't make it part of this task. Rules you control beat explanations you don't.

  • It could match text, but that isn't the point of the scope check.

Show answer

B. "Swap flask for fastapi" explains the step but doesn't make it part of this task. Rules you control beat explanations you don't.

Key takeaways

  • Ask for plans as JSON so code can check them, and reject replies that don't parse, with a reason.
  • Compare every path against the real file list (git ls-files) to catch invented files.
  • Scope and protected paths are your rules; the model's reasons don't override them.
  • A test run must come after the last change, not just somewhere in the plan.
  • Use severities: BLOCK sends a plan back, WARN and ASK go to a human, and a clean result still means "review the diff later."

#Ideas to extend it

  • Read the protected patterns from AGENTS.md instead of hard-coding them, for example from lines that start with Never edit.
  • Add a check that every bug-fix plan edits a test file before it edits the code it tests.
  • Cap the plan size: more than 10 changes for a one-function bug is itself a finding.
  • Feed the findings back to a scripted model as a message and check its second plan.

#Further reading

  • git ls-files (opens in a new tab): the real source of the file list, including how to list untracked files that an agent created.
  • json (opens in a new tab): JSONDecodeError and its msg, lineno, and colno attributes, useful for telling a model exactly where its reply broke.

What you'll learn

  • Turn claims from an AI's repository map into searches, and read the results correctly.

Most exercises use the same small shop repository, so its files are in the first solution and reused after that. Each solution is self-contained: copy it, run it, then change the inputs and see what breaks.

#Warm-up: what kind of claim is this?

Check your understanding

3 questions

1"The Order class is defined in shop/models.py." What's the cheapest way to check it?

  • One search shows every file that defines it, including the case where it's defined twice.

  • Tests can pass whether or not this claim is true; they don't tell you where a class lives.

  • The same model rereading the same context tends to repeat the same answer.

Show answer

A. One search shows every file that defines it, including the case where it's defined twice.

2"Nothing reads the LEGACY_MODE setting anymore." What kind of claim is it, and how much do you trust a search with no hits?

  • It's a claim that something doesn't exist, which is the hard kind.

  • Code like os.environ["LEGACY_" + mode] can read it without the full name ever appearing.

Show answer

B. Code like os.environ["LEGACY_" + mode] can read it without the full name ever appearing.

3"apply_coupon returns the total unchanged for unknown codes." How do you check it?

  • The search finds where it's used, not what it does.

  • Behavior claims need the code to run. Searching only answers where things are.

Show answer

B. Behavior claims need the code to run. Searching only answers where things are.

#Exercise 1: Count the real call sites

The AI's map says: "apply_coupon is called in exactly one place, shop/checkout.py." Write call_sites(files, name) that returns file:line for every line calling name(, excluding the line that defines it. Make sure apply_coupon_v2( doesn't count as a call to apply_coupon.

Need a hint?

\b in a regex marks a word boundary, and ( must be escaped as \(. Since _ counts as a word character, \bapply_coupon\( doesn't match apply_coupon_v2(. Skip lines whose stripped text starts with def .

Show solution

Three call sites, not one. The import lines don't count because they have no ( after the name. The one in cart.py is the interesting miss: apply_coupon_v2 calls the original, so changing apply_coupon's behavior changes v2 too, which a fix based on the AI's claim would never test. re.escape makes the function safe for names containing regex characters.

#Exercise 2: Catch the invented paths

Here is part of an AI's repository map and the repository's tracked files:

Write invented_paths(text, tracked) that finds every path-like string in the map and returns the ones that don't exist.

Need a hint?

A path here is a run of letters, digits, _, ., /, or -, followed by a dot and an extension: [\w./-]+\.\w+. A sentence-ending period can stick to the match, so strip trailing dots. Then it's a set difference.

Show solution

Look at the shapes of the three mistakes. receipt.html is a near miss of the real receipt.txt. test_checkout.py is the file that should exist by naming convention, so the model assumed it did, which also tells you checkout has no tests. coupons.json is invented outright. Pattern-completion errors like these are why every path in a map gets checked.

#Exercise 3: Critique this plan

Task: "Add a --dry-run flag to cleanup.py that prints which old log files would be deleted, without deleting them." The agent's plan:

Write down at least four problems, and say which one you'd raise first.

Need a hint?

Which step changes real data? Which steps aren't part of the task? Where is the evidence that the flag works? What is the plan assuming about the code?

Show solution
  • Step 1 is the one to raise first. Running the script without the flag deletes the log files, the exact thing the task is trying to avoid. Read the code instead, or run it on a copied folder.
  • Step 2 is scope creep with a cost. Switching libraries adds a dependency and changes every flag's behavior, and the task never asked for it.
  • Step 3 is vague. "Add --dry-run" doesn't say what the dry run prints or which code path it skips.
  • Step 4 changes shared infrastructure. CI configuration affects everyone. It's out of scope and needs its own approval.
  • Step 5 claims success without evidence. There's no test, for example one that creates temporary old files, runs with --dry-run, and checks that every file still exists.
  • Hidden assumption: that the script uses argparse at all, and that nothing else imports it. Neither was checked.

Step 1 goes first because it's the only step that can cause harm Git can't undo: deleted log files were never in the repository.

#Exercise 4: Check a "safe to delete" claim

The AI says three functions are unused and safe to delete: apply_coupon_v2, send_welcome, and format_total. Write references(files, name) that finds every line in any tracked file (not only .py files) that mentions the name as a whole word, other than its own def line. Then report on each claim.

Need a hint?

Search for the bare name with \bname\b, not name(. One of these functions is never called with parentheses in the code, only named in a string.

Show solution

send_welcome is reached through a string in HANDLERS and a globals() lookup, so searching for send_welcome( would have missed it. format_total is used only by a template, which an AI that read only Python files would never see. And "no references" for apply_coupon_v2 still only covers this repository: another project could import it, which is why deleting a public function is a question for a human.

#Exercise 5: Add a tests-first rule to the plan checker

For a bug fix, the safest plan changes a test before it changes the code (so the test can fail first). Write check_test_first(steps) that returns a WARN finding if the first .py file a plan edits isn't a test file (test_*.py).

Need a hint?

Walk the steps in order and stop at the first edit of a .py file. If it's a test file, there's nothing to report; otherwise return one finding with that step's number.

Show solution

It's a WARN, not a BLOCK, because some correct plans edit code first (a pure refactor with existing tests, for instance). The rule is a prompt for a question: "how will you know the bug was there before your fix?"

#Exercise 6: Questions before a risky plan

An agent's plan for "Speed up the orders page" includes this step:

Write four questions you'd want answered before approving step 4.

Need a hint?

Think about data that can't come back, about what "unused" was based on, about how the change reaches the real database, and about how you'd know it helped.

Show solution
  1. How do we know notes is unused? Which search was run, and did it cover reports, admin tools, and other services that read the same database?
  2. Can it be undone? Dropping a column deletes its data. Is there a backup, and does the migration have a working reverse step?
  3. Where does this run first? On a copy of production data, or straight against the real database? How long does building the index take on the real table size, and does it lock writes while it runs?
  4. What's the evidence it's faster? Which query is slow today, how long does it take, and what number counts as fixed?

A good outcome is often to split the step: approve the index (reversible, directly tied to the task) and send the column drop back as its own reviewed change.

#Challenge: Steps out of order and circular plans

Some agents return plans as a graph: each step has an id and an after list of steps it depends on. Write order_problems(steps) that reports (1) any step listed before a step it depends on, (2) any dependency that isn't in the plan, and (3) a dependency cycle, if there is one.

Need a hint?

Map each id to its position in the list; a dependency with a larger position than the step is out of order. For cycles, do a depth-first walk along after links while keeping the current path. Reaching a node that's already on the path means you've found a cycle.

Show solution

path + [node] builds a new list on each call instead of changing a shared one, so every branch of the search keeps its own path. A cycle in a plan is never a reordering problem: no order can satisfy it, so it goes back to the agent with the cycle spelled out. For large plans you'd want Python's built-in graphlib.TopologicalSorter, which raises CycleError on the same input.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read a unified diff: file headers, hunk headers, context, removed and added lines.
  • Check a change's shape (which files, how big, tests or config touched) before reading its lines.
  • Spot the changes that most often hide problems: weakened tests, swallowed failures, special-cased inputs.
  • Say what counts as verification evidence, and use a linter and a type checker to catch what tests miss.

The agent's summary is short and sure of itself: "Fixed to_dollars so amounts always show two decimal places. All tests pass." Then you run git diff --stat:

A formatting fix touched the CI configuration? You scroll up in the agent's terminal and find the last line of its own test run: FAILED (failures=1). The summary, the diff, and the evidence tell three different stories, and only two of them are facts. This lesson is about reading those two.

#Reading a unified diff

A diff is a list of instructions for turning the old file into the new one. Python's difflib writes the same unified format as git diff, so you can make one from two strings:

Read it top to bottom:

  • --- a/money.py and +++ b/money.py name the old and new versions of the file.
  • @@ -1,6 +1,6 @@ is a hunk header: this chunk covers 6 lines starting at line 1 in the old file, and 6 lines starting at line 1 in the new one. When the two counts differ, the change added or removed lines.
  • Lines starting with a space are context, unchanged and shown so you can see where you are.
  • - lines were removed and + lines were added. A changed line shows up as one of each.

git diff adds a diff --git line and an index line per file, and often the enclosing function name after the second @@. Otherwise it's the same format.

#Check the shape before the lines

Before reading a single +, look at git diff --stat and ask:

  1. Are these the files I expected? Compare with the task's scope.
  2. Did tests change? Fine if tests were added. A reason to slow down if existing ones were edited.
  3. Did configuration, CI, or dependency files change? Those affect everyone, not just this feature.
  4. Is the size proportional? A one-line bug with a 400-line diff needs an explanation.

The hook's diff fails questions 2 and 3. Here's what it actually says:

Three problems, one per file. round(10.0, 2) is still 10.0, so the "fix" changes nothing for whole dollars or for 1050 (still $10.5). The test's expected value was edited to match the broken output. And || true makes the CI step succeed even when the tests fail, so the build would show green forever.

#Changes that deserve a second look

These patterns are worth a pause in any diff, and they come up often in agent-written code because they're quick ways to make a failing check stop failing:

  • Edited expectations. An assertEqual whose expected value changed in the same diff as the code it tests.
  • Removed or skipped tests. Deleted test methods, @unittest.skip, pytest.mark.skip, or a test body replaced by pass.
  • Swallowed failures. except Exception: pass, a bare except:, || true in a script, or continue-on-error in CI.
  • Special cases that match the test inputs. if cents == 1050: return "$10.50" passes the test and fixes nothing.
  • New dependencies for something the standard library already does.
  • Comments that promise more than the code does, like # handles all currencies above a line that hard-codes $.

#Plausible but wrong

The hardest bugs to catch in review are fixes that look right and pass the tests they were given. A bug report says is_leap(1900) wrongly returns True. The agent adds and year % 100 != 0. The existing tests (2024, 2023, 1900) all pass. Before stepping through, predict what it says about 2000.

2000 was a leap year: years divisible by 400 are the exception to the exception. The fix handled the case in the bug report and broke one nobody tested. The defense is to write a test for the neighbors of every bug (here, 2000 and 2100) before accepting the fix. You'll do exactly that in the next lesson.

#Evidence you can trust

"All tests pass" is a sentence. Evidence is something you could reproduce:

Claim Evidence
"Tests pass" The exact command, its full output, and the exit code
"I ran them after the fix" The run comes after the last edit, ideally tied to a commit hash
"Nothing else changed" git diff --stat matches the files in the task
"I added tests" The new test names appear in the diff and in the -v output

Know what the end of a unittest run can say, because two of the endings look like success and aren't:

Check the exit code yourself right after a run: echo $? in bash and zsh, $LASTEXITCODE in PowerShell. Zero means success. Best of all, don't rely on anyone's report: run the command yourself, on the final code.

#Linters and type checkers catch what tests don't

Tests only check the paths they run. This file has a typo in a branch no test exercises and a type mistake in a function nobody has called yet:

A test calling receipt_line("Tea", 250) passes. Two optional tools, installed into your course environment with python -m pip install ruff mypy, find the rest without running anything. Ruff is a fast linter:

mypy reads the type hints and checks that calls match them:

Line 15 is a real bug: values read from a CSV are strings, and "250" / 100 raises TypeError the first time anyone uses it. Both tools exit with code 1 when they find problems, so they make good acceptance criteria: "ruff check . and mypy . report no errors."

⚠️ Watch out

Reviewing the summary instead of the diff. The summary is the agent's description of its intent, written by the same process that made the change. Read git diff --stat first and the summary last, if at all.

⚠️ Watch out

Trusting a green CI badge. Green means the configured commands exited with 0. If the diff changed those commands (|| true, a skip flag, a narrower test path), green tells you nothing. Always read CI changes with extra care.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A hunk header reads @@ -10,4 +10,6 @@. What does it tell you?

  • The numbers after the commas are line counts, not line numbers.

  • -start,count describes the old file and +start,count the new one.

  • The header describes this chunk only, not the whole file.

Show answer

B. -start,count describes the old file and +start,count the new one.

2The diff for a bug fix changes money.py and also changes an expected value in tests/test_money.py. What should you do?

  • Adding tests is normal. Changing what an existing test expects, in the same change as the code, is how broken code gets a passing test.

  • Sometimes the old test really was wrong, but that needs a reason you can verify, not the agent's word.

  • You'd merge code whose test you haven't seen pass. Understand the change first.

Show answer

B. Sometimes the old test really was wrong, but that needs a reason you can verify, not the agent's word.

3An agent reports its test run ended with OK (skipped=2). What does that tell you?

  • Skipped tests didn't run at all, so they neither passed nor failed.

  • A skip added in the same diff as a fix is the same red flag as an edited expectation.

  • It's a valid run; it's just incomplete evidence.

Show answer

B. A skip added in the same diff as a fix is the same red flag as an edited expectation.

4Why did the is_leap fix pass review-by-tests?

  • 2000 is the neighboring case that the new condition breaks, and nobody tested it.

  • % works the same for every integer here; the logic is what's wrong.

  • The trace ran the real function; the problem is which inputs were checked.

Show answer

A. 2000 is the neighboring case that the new condition breaks, and nobody tested it.

Key takeaways

  • In @@ -a,b +c,d @@, a and c are starting lines, b and d are line counts for the old and new versions.
  • Check the shape first: expected files, edited tests, changed config or dependencies, proportional size.
  • Edited expectations, skips, swallowed failures, and special cases are the usual ways a failing check gets silenced.
  • Evidence is a reproducible command, its full output, and its exit code, run after the last edit, preferably by you.
  • Linters and type checkers find errors on paths your tests never run.

#Further reading

  • What to look for in a code review (opens in a new tab): Google's short, practical checklist, from design down to comments.
  • git diff (opens in a new tab): the options worth learning first are --stat, --staged, and main...your-branch.
  • Ruff (opens in a new tab) and mypy (opens in a new tab): setup and the rule lists behind the error codes above.
