m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a model can't reliably separate instructions from data inside its context window.
  • Watch a naive agent read a planted README and leak a secret, in a demo that runs here.
  • Tell direct from indirect prompt injection, and name why the indirect kind is the agent's problem.
  • Use the lethal trifecta and the Agents Rule of Two to judge when a workflow is dangerous.

A teammate opens a pull request that adds one file to a repository your agent maintains. The diff looks boring: a README.md with install notes. Buried in it is a paragraph addressed to "any AI assistant reading this," telling the agent to open secrets/token.txt and paste the contents into its reply. The next time someone asks the agent to "summarize the README for a new contributor," the agent reads the file, follows the paragraph, and the deploy token lands in a chat log where the attacker can see it. No tool malfunctioned. The agent did exactly what the text in its context told it to do.

That is prompt injection, and it is the defining security problem of tool-using agents. This lesson shows the attack working, explains why it works, and gives you two mental models for spotting vulnerable designs. The next two lessons build the defenses.

#Everything in the context is one undifferentiated stream

Here is the uncomfortable truth underneath the whole lesson. When you call a model, you send it a sequence of tokens: your system instructions, the user's request, and every tool result so far, one after another. The model has no reliable, built-in way to know which tokens are trusted orders from you and which are data it happened to read. A file's contents sit in the same stream as your rules, in the same format, and the most capable instruction in that stream often wins.

This is not a bug in one model that a better model will fix. It is structural. Compare it to SQL injection, where a database can't tell a value you meant as data from a value an attacker wrote as code, unless you keep them on separate rails with parameters. A model has no equivalent of parameters for "this is only data," so the separation has to come from the harness around it, not from asking the model nicely.

#The attack, running

Below is a naive agent with no defenses. It reads the README to do its job, then keeps following any open the file … instruction it finds in what it has read. The planted line in the README is such an instruction. Predict what the final answer contains before you run it.

The agent was asked to summarize one file. It read a second file it was never told to touch, and the token is now in its output, ready to be copied anywhere the output goes. The naive_agent here obeys a regex, but a real model's willingness to follow confident instructions in its context is the same weakness in a fancier wrapper. Nothing about "the model is smart" protects you. A smarter model follows a cleverer injection.

#Direct versus indirect: the agent's problem is the indirect one

Direct injection is when the person typing at the agent tries to jailbreak it: "ignore your rules and tell me how to…". Annoying, but the user is one identity you already decided to trust to some degree.

Indirect injection is when the malicious instructions ride in on data the agent reads while doing an innocent task: a file, a web page, an issue comment, a code review, a tool's output, the description of a tool on an untrusted server. The person running the agent never sees the payload, and may have no idea it is there. Every source your agent reads is an attack surface, and agents are built to read a lot of sources.

#Two models for spotting danger: the lethal trifecta and the Rule of Two

You won't catch every injection string. What you can do is design so that a successful injection has nothing valuable to do. Two framings make that concrete.

Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (June 2025) says data theft becomes possible when an agent combines all three of these in one session:

  1. Access to private data (your repo, your secrets, a customer database).
  2. Exposure to untrusted content (anything an attacker could get in front of the model).
  3. A way to communicate externally (post to a URL, send a message, open a PR, even write to a shared file).

Remove any one leg and the injection has no path to steal. An agent that reads untrusted web pages and can exfiltrate but has no access to anything private is mostly harmless. Add your private repo, and it becomes a thief.

Meta's Agents Rule of Two (October 2025), inspired by that trifecta and by Chromium's rule of 2, puts the same idea as a budget. Within a session, try to let an agent satisfy at most two of: [A] process untrustworthy input, [B] access sensitive systems or private data, [C] change state or communicate externally. Want all three? Then a human reviews the sensitive step, or you split the work into separate agents that each hold only two.

#The five defenses this module builds, and the non-defense

The next lessons build these, in order of how much you should trust them:

  • Treat every tool result as data, never as orders. The harness never parses tool output for commands to run. Only the model proposes calls, and your gate decides.
  • An allowlist of tools scoped to the task, so there is no outbound tool to misuse in the first place.
  • A path sandbox with a never-touch list, so secrets/ and .env can't be read even when the model asks.
  • An exfiltration check on the arguments of any outbound tool, so a secret can't leave even if it was somehow read.
  • Human approval for the handful of external, irreversible actions, bound to the exact call.

Notice what is not on the list: "add a sentence to the system prompt telling the model to ignore injected instructions." That helps a little and fails often, because it is one instruction competing with an attacker's instruction in the same stream. Treat it as a speed bump, not a wall.

⚠️ Watch out

Be suspicious of any product that promises to "detect and block 95% of prompt injections." In application security, 95% is a failing grade: an attacker just tries a hundred variations and two get through. Filters that scan for bad phrases are worth having as one layer, but a design where injection has nothing to steal beats a filter that is right most of the time. Build so that the attack is pointless, not merely usually caught.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Why can't you fix injection by telling the model, in the system prompt, to ignore any instructions found in files?

  • They are, but a system instruction is one more line in the same context, competing with the attacker's line.

  • The model weighs both as text. A confident injection often wins, which is why the separation must come from the harness.

  • Length isn't the issue; the lack of a hard data/instruction boundary is.

Show answer

B. The model weighs both as text. A confident injection often wins, which is why the separation must come from the harness.

2An agent reads untrusted web pages, holds no private data, and can post to any URL. By the lethal trifecta, how worried should you be about data theft?

  • Posting alone can't steal data the agent never had access to.

  • Two legs present, one missing. Injection can make it post junk, but not exfiltrate your secrets.

  • It can still be made to post misleading or attacker-chosen content, and reading untrusted pages has other risks. "Less worried about theft" is not "safe".

Show answer

B. Two legs present, one missing. Injection can make it post junk, but not exfiltrate your secrets.

3Which of these is indirect prompt injection?

  • That's direct injection: the instruction comes from the person at the keyboard.

  • The payload arrives in data the agent reads for a normal task, from someone who never talks to the agent directly.

  • That's a correctness failure, not an injected instruction from an attacker.

Show answer

B. The payload arrives in data the agent reads for a normal task, from someone who never talks to the agent directly.

4The Agents Rule of Two suggests an agent should satisfy at most two of three properties in a session. What do you do when a task genuinely needs all three?

  • Needing all three is exactly when an injection can steal; trust isn't a control.

  • Either break the chain with review or make sure no single agent combines all three unsupervised.

  • That removes your audit trail and does nothing about the exfiltration path.

Show answer

B. Either break the chain with review or make sure no single agent combines all three unsupervised.

Key takeaways

  • A model reads its system rules, the user request, and tool output as one stream; it has no built-in boundary marking "data, not orders."
  • Indirect prompt injection hides instructions in content the agent reads for a normal task, so the user never sees the payload.
  • Data theft needs all three of the lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content, and a way to communicate out. Remove one leg.
  • The Rule of Two is the same idea as a budget: at most two of untrusted input, sensitive access, and external action per session, or add a human.
  • Defend by making injection pointless (sandbox, allowlist, exfiltration check, approval), not by asking the model to ignore it.

#Further reading

  • The lethal trifecta for AI agents (opens in a new tab): Simon Willison's short, clear statement of the three-way combination that makes agents exfiltrate data, and why vendor filters don't save you.
  • Agents Rule of Two (opens in a new tab): Meta's practical framing of the same risk as a per-session budget, with worked examples of safe and unsafe tool combinations.
  • OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection (opens in a new tab): the canonical catalog entry, with direct and indirect variants and a list of partial mitigations.

m7-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Hand every tool result back to the model wrapped as data, and keep the harness from ever executing instructions found in output.
  • Confine reads to a sandbox with a never-touch list, so planted instructions can't reach secrets/.
  • Scan the arguments of outbound tools and block any call that carries a secret, before a human is even asked.
  • Record every decision in an audit log, then run a compromised model and confirm the secret never leaves.

In the last lesson a naive agent read a planted README and leaked a token. Now you build the gate that stops it. The design assumes the model is already compromised: the attacker's instructions are in its context, and it will try to read a secret and post it to a server it controls. Your job is to make every one of those steps fail, and to leave a record of the attempt.

The cells share state like a notebook, so run them in order. On your own machine, paste them into one file (safe_agent.py); the finished version is at the end.

#Step 1: A repo carrying an injection, and a secret in the environment

The repo holds a README.md with a planted instruction, some real source, and a secrets/deploy.key the agent should never open. The harness process also carries a live token in its environment, the way a developer's shell often does.

#Step 2: Tools, a task profile, and a path sandbox

Three tools, and a profile that says which the agent may name, what each reads or writes, and what it must never touch. read_file enforces the sandbox itself, because containment depends on the real filesystem, not on the shape of a string (the point you proved in Module 6). http_post is simulated: it appends to SENT so you can see exactly what would have left the machine.

The last two lines are the sandbox doing its job: the README reads fine, and the secret the injection wants is refused by the never-list before any bytes come back.

#Step 3: An exfiltration check on outgoing arguments

Suppose the model reads a secret some other way, or already has one from its environment. The last line of defense is to look at what is about to leave. exfiltration_reason scans an outbound call's arguments for the value of any sensitive environment variable and for text shaped like a credential. It is deliberately simple and will miss cleverly encoded secrets (the practice lesson attacks exactly that), so it is a layer, not the whole wall.

A secret-carrying call gets a reason; a clean status update gets None. The check runs before any human is asked, and it fails closed, for a reason worth stating plainly: an injected instruction can write a very convincing cover story, and a tired reviewer might approve "posting a verification token to the maintainers." Don't give them the chance.

#Step 4: Wrap output as data, and gate every call

Two more pieces. as_data wraps a tool result in a labeled envelope before it goes back to the model, a reminder that the content is data, not orders. It is defense in depth: the model may still ignore the label, which is why the structural checks above do the real work. The harness itself never reads tool output looking for commands to run; only the model proposes calls, and gated_execute decides.

#Step 5: Send a compromised model through the gate

Here is the model acting on the injection: read the README, read the secret, post the environment token to the attacker's URL, then write an innocent-looking summary. Watch each hostile step fail and the audit log fill up.

Three things to read off the output. The secret read came back as an error, stopped by the sandbox. The http_post was denied by the exfiltration check, and notice the human was never asked, even though the scripted reviewer was set to approve. And SENT is empty: nothing left the machine. The model did its worst and accomplished nothing.

#Step 6: Prove the gate still lets good work through

A gate that denies everything is easy and useless. A legitimate outbound call, with no secret in it, passes the exfiltration check and reaches a human, who can approve it.

This time the exfiltration check finds nothing, the human approves the exact call, and the ping goes out. The audit log records the decision and its reason either way, which is what makes the whole run reviewable afterward.

#The finished agent

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The compromised model's http_post was denied before the human was asked, even though the scripted reviewer would have approved. Why skip the human?

  • Speed isn't the point; the exfiltration check is about not trusting a human to catch a disguised secret.

  • Removing the human from a call that already looks like theft is safer than hoping they notice.

  • A missing reason isn't why it was denied; the secret in the body is.

Show answer

B. Removing the human from a call that already looks like theft is safer than hoping they notice.

2read_file("secrets/deploy.key") returned an error, not the file. Which layer stopped it, and why there?

  • The exfiltration check looks at outbound arguments, not at file reads.

  • Containment and the never-list are checked inside the tool, since they depend on the real filesystem.

  • read_file is allowed; the specific path is what was refused.

Show answer

B. Containment and the never-list are checked inside the tool, since they depend on the real filesystem.

3Why wrap tool output in a <<TOOL OUTPUT ... DATA>> envelope if the model might ignore the label?

  • It guarantees nothing; a model can ignore it, which is why the structural checks exist.

  • Layers that don't rely on the model's cooperation do the real work; the label is a bonus.

  • The harness never executes instructions found in output; only the model proposes calls.

Show answer

B. Layers that don't rely on the model's cooperation do the real work; the label is a bonus.

Key takeaways

  • Assume the model is already compromised, and make each hostile step fail: read blocked, exfiltration blocked, approval required.
  • The path sandbox enforces containment inside the tool; the exfiltration check guards what leaves; approval covers the rest.
  • Run the exfiltration check before asking a human, and fail closed, because an injected reason can be persuasive.
  • Wrap tool output as data for defense in depth, but never let the harness execute instructions it finds in output.
  • An audit log of every decision and reason is what makes the whole run reviewable after the fact.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a write_file tool in the write tier, and confirm the never-list still refuses writes to secrets/.
  • Have exfiltration_reason also flag any argument that contains a chunk of text read earlier from a never path, not just known patterns.
  • Count outbound calls per task and deny once a small budget is spent, so a flood of "harmless" posts can't drain data slowly.
  • Make the audit log tamper-evident with a hash chain (the practice lesson's challenge), so a compromised run can't quietly edit its own record.

#Further reading

  • OWASP LLM Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet (opens in a new tab): concrete defenses, including least privilege, output handling, and human-in-the-loop for high-impact actions.
  • MCP security best practices (opens in a new tab): the local-server compromise section, consent dialogs that show the exact command, and sandboxing guidance.
  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet (opens in a new tab): what belongs in a security-relevant event log, and what must never be written into one.

m7-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Redact secrets from logs and refuse to send a prompt that contains one.
  • Beat a weak exfiltration check that misses an encoded secret.
  • Flag typosquatted package names and dependencies that aren't pinned or hashed.
  • Find instructions hidden in a tool description, including invisible characters, and build a tamper-evident log.

Each exercise starts from something that looks safe and isn't. Run the attacks for real before reading the solution: an encoded secret, a package name one letter off, and an instruction made of invisible characters all pass a casual glance, and the only way to trust a check is to throw the nasty input at it.

#Warm-up: predict the gap

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You scrub a log line by replacing known secret patterns with [REDACTED]. The line also holds the exact value of $GITHUB_TOKEN, which happens not to match any pattern. What's the most reliable way to catch it?

  • You'll always be one format behind; the token's shape may be unknown to you.

  • You hold those strings, so an exact replace can't miss them, whatever shape they take.

  • Encryption protects the file at rest; it does nothing about the plaintext you pass to a model or a chat.

Show answer

B. You hold those strings, so an exact replace can't miss them, whatever shape they take.

2A requirements line reads flask>=2.0. Why is that a supply-chain risk even when you install from the official index?

  • The source index is the same; the version range is the problem.

  • A pinned, hashed requirement installs exactly the artifact you reviewed and nothing else.

  • Any distribution can be hashed; being pure Python has nothing to do with it.

Show answer

B. A pinned, hashed requirement installs exactly the artifact you reviewed and nothing else.

#Exercise 1: Redact secrets before they reach a log

Write redact(text) for the harness's logger. It must replace the exact values of sensitive environment variables and anything shaped like a credential. Prove it on a log line that contains a real (fake) token.

Need a hint?

Replace the environment values first (you know them exactly), then run pattern substitutions for shapes like ghp_…, AKIA…, and key: value. Doing the exact values first gives the clearer label.

Show solution

Replacing the known environment value first turns it into the readable [GITHUB_TOKEN] label, and the pattern pass is the backstop for secrets you don't hold, such as one pasted into an error message. Redaction is for logs and transcripts; it is not a license to put secrets near the model in the first place.

#Exercise 2: Refuse to send a prompt that leaks a secret

Secrets belong in environment variables, never pasted into a prompt. Write assert_no_secret(prompt) that raises if the assembled prompt contains the value of any sensitive variable, and wire it into a tiny build_prompt. Show it passing a clean prompt and blocking a poisoned one.

Need a hint?

You already know the exact secret strings from the environment. A substring test over the full prompt is enough; no regex needed.

Show solution

This catches the common accident where a secret rides into the prompt through a user message or a tool result. It runs just before you call the model, so a leak is stopped at the last moment instead of being discovered later in a transcript.

#Exercise 3: Beat a check that misses an encoded secret

The exfiltration check from the build-along looks for a secret verbatim. An attacker encodes it first. Show that the simple substring check misses a base64-encoded token, then write strong_check that decodes base64-looking chunks and rescans.

Need a hint?

Find runs of base64 characters with a regex, pad each to a multiple of four, try to decode, and look for the secret in the decoded text. Catch decode errors and move on.

Show solution

Encoding is why pattern-matching alone can't be your only wall. For every trick you decode, there's another (hex, zlib, splitting the secret across two arguments), which is the real argument for removing the secret's access entirely: a secret the agent can never read can't be encoded and smuggled out.

#Exercise 4: Flag typosquatted packages

An agent proposes installing a list of packages. Write screen(name) that passes names on your project's allowlist, blocks a name within one edit of a popular package (a classic typosquat), and flags anything else for review.

Need a hint?

Write a small Levenshtein distance. A typosquat is usually one deletion, insertion, or substitution away from a real name, so distance exactly 1 to a popular package is the signal.

Show solution

The allowlist is the real defense: an agent should install from a reviewed set, not from whatever name it typed. The distance check adds a loud warning for the specific, common trick of a name that looks almost right, which is how slopsquatting works when a model hallucinates a plausible-but-wrong package name.

#Exercise 5: Audit a requirements file for pinning and hashes

Write audit(line) that classifies each requirement as pinned-and-hashed, pinned-but-not-hashed, or not pinned. Reproducible, reviewable installs need both an exact version and a hash.

Need a hint?

The package name is the text before the first comparison or space. == means pinned; --hash= means hashed. Skip blank lines and comments.

Show solution

With hashes present, pip switches into hash-checking mode and refuses any dependency that isn't pinned and hashed, so one --hash protects the whole tree. For tools you run rather than install, the same idea is pinning an exact version (for example uvx --from 'ruff==0.3.0' ruff check) instead of taking whatever is newest.

#Exercise 6: Find the instruction hidden in a tool description

A malicious MCP server ships a tool whose visible description is innocent, but whose text carries hidden instructions, some in plain sight and some in invisible Unicode tag characters. Write screen_description(desc) that decodes the hidden characters and flags suspicious phrases.

Need a hint?

Unicode tag characters live in U+E0000 to U+E007F and render as nothing. Subtract 0xE0000 from each to recover the ASCII it was built from, then search the visible and hidden text together for red-flag phrases.

Show solution

The visible description is a friendly calculator; the hidden half tells the model to exfiltrate .env. This is a tool poisoning attack, and it is why you show users the full, decoded description of every tool, pin a server's tool definitions, and re-check them against a hash so a server can't quietly swap a safe description for a hostile one later.

#Challenge: A tamper-evident audit log

An audit log is only evidence if nobody can quietly edit it. Build a hash chain: each entry stores the hash of the previous one, so changing or deleting any entry breaks every hash after it. Write chain(entries) and verify(log), then prove that editing one entry is detected.

Need a hint?

Each record is {"prev": previous_hash, "event": entry}, and its hash is sha256 of the canonical JSON of that record. verify walks the log, recomputing each hash and checking the prev link.

Show solution

Editing entry 1 leaves its stored hash unchanged, so the recomputed hash no longer matches and verify names the exact entry. Deleting an entry breaks the prev link of the next one. Keep the log append-only and, for real stakes, write each line to storage the agent's own account can't rewrite, so a compromised run can't launder its own history.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Know exactly what your agent must do and what you hand in.
  • Pick one of four projects at a difficulty you can finish, with room to grow.
  • Plan the agent on a template: task profile, tools, scopes, approvals, and the report it produces.
  • Write a threat model that maps each untrusted input to the control that stops it.

For seven modules you reviewed agents other people designed and attacked harnesses someone else wrote. The capstone is yours. You build an agent that works on a sandbox repository and comes back with a result you can trust, even when the repository is trying to trick it. Everything runs offline against the scripted fake model from Modules 5 through 7, so you are building the harness, not renting a model.

The projects below differ in ambition, but they share one spine: a validated tool loop, a permission gate, defenses against injected content, and an auditable report. The best capstones in past cohorts were not the most ambitious. They were the ones where someone picked a scope they could actually finish and then spent their time making the gate airtight and the threat model honest.

#What your agent must do

Whichever project you pick, the agent has to show all of these, because each one is a lesson from this course made real:

Requirement Where it came from
A tool loop with a hard step cap Modules 2 and 5
Tool definitions with JSON Schema, validated before running Module 5
A path sandbox with a never-touch list Module 6
A command allowlist and tiered tools (read, write, external) Module 6
Human approval for the external tier, bound to the exact call Module 6
Tool output treated as data, plus an exfiltration check Module 7
An audit log of every decision, and a report the harness writes Module 7

#What you hand in

  1. A program that runs offline against a scripted model and finishes without crashing.
  2. A threat model (the template is below): assets, untrusted inputs, trust boundaries, and the control for each path.
  3. A red-team test suite that proves the attacks in your threat model are blocked, and that normal work still gets through. Lesson 3 walks you through writing it.
  4. A short demo, 3 to 5 minutes, where you run the agent, trigger one blocked attack, and show the audit log.

#Pick a project

Choose one. Each can be finished with the skeleton in the next lesson; the difficulty is in how much the agent is trusted to change.

1. Docs typo fixer (starter). The agent reads docs/, fixes a spelling error in one Markdown file, runs a spellcheck command, and reports. Write scope is docs/*.md only. This is the Module 6 gate wrapped in a loop and a report. Good if you want to make one gate perfect.

2. Failing-test fixer (core). The agent reads a failing test and the source it covers, makes a scoped edit to src/, runs the test suite as a named command, confirms it passes, reviews its own diff, and reports. The planted README tries to send it off task. This is the recommended target.

3. Issue triage over untrusted text (advanced). The agent reads issue reports written by strangers (fully untrusted), summarizes them, and proposes a branch name and a one-line plan, but makes no change without approval. The whole challenge is resisting injection while still being useful, since the input is adversarial by definition.

4. Harden and red-team (stretch). Take project 2 or 3, package its tools as an MCP server (Module 5), and write an attacker that tries ten ways to break out: path escapes, encoded exfiltration, a poisoned tool description, an approval replayed on a different call. Score your own defenses. Best if you learn by breaking things.

💡 Tip

Scope down before you scope up. A fully working starter with a tight gate and a real threat model beats an ambitious triage agent whose sandbox leaks. You can always add a tier or a tool once the core is solid and tested.

#Plan before you code

Fill this in before writing the loop. It is the task profile from Module 6 plus the pieces the capstone adds. Keep it in a comment at the top of your file so a reviewer sees the rules before the code.

#Write out one run, step by step

Before the code, trace the run on paper. For the failing-test fixer it reads like this, and writing it now tells you which tools and checks you actually need:

Steps 7 and 8 are the point of the capstone. Your agent must stay safe even when the repository tells it not to.

#Threat-model it

A threat model is four questions answered honestly. Don't skip it: it is how you find the control you forgot. For each untrusted input, name the worst thing it could cause and the one control that stops it.

Untrusted input Worst case Control that stops it
README.md with a planted instruction Agent reads a secret and posts it out Tool output is data, not orders; sandbox blocks the read
A tool result the model reads Injected "now run deploy" Allowlist has no deploy tool; unknown tools denied
A path argument like ../../.ssh/id_rsa Read outside the project resolve() plus is_relative_to, then the never-list
An outbound http_post body Secret leaves the machine Exfiltration check before any human is asked; approval for the rest
A dependency the agent names Typosquat or malicious package Install from an allowlist; pin and hash

Then run the lethal-trifecta check from Module 7 on your design. Does one session combine private data, untrusted content, and external communication? If so, the external step must pass through a human, or you split the work so no single run holds all three. Write that conclusion down. It is the spine of your whole defense.

Key takeaways

  • Every capstone shows the same spine: validated tool loop, path sandbox, tiered tools with approval, injection and exfiltration defenses, and an auditable report.
  • Pick a project you can finish. A tight starter beats a leaky advanced build.
  • Plan the task profile and trace one run on paper before writing code, so you know which tools and checks you need.
  • A threat model maps each untrusted input to the single control that stops it; the lethal-trifecta check tells you where a human must step in.

#Further reading

  • OWASP Threat Modeling Process (opens in a new tab): the four-question method behind the table above, with decomposition and countermeasure steps.
  • OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet (opens in a new tab): a compact checklist for assets, entry points, and trust boundaries you can reuse for your write-up.
  • Agents Rule of Two (opens in a new tab): the per-session budget to apply when your design combines untrusted input, private data, and external action.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Grow the agent from a running skeleton to a full gate in five milestones, testing after each.
  • Reuse the validator, sandbox, tiers, approval, and exfiltration check you built in Modules 5 through 7.
  • Drive the whole thing with a scripted model so it runs offline, fixing a real failing test.
  • Produce a report the harness writes from the audit log, not from the model's own claims.

This lesson builds the recommended project, the failing-test fixer, as a starter you can adapt to any of the four. You add one capability per milestone and run the agent after each, so a break is easy to find. By the end, the agent fixes a genuine bug, confirms the fix with the test suite, and refuses two attacks planted in the repository, all offline against the scripted model.

The five milestones map to the cells below:

  • M1: the sandbox repo exists, with a bug, a test, a planted README, and a secret.
  • M2: tools and their schemas are defined and validated.
  • M3: the gate decides allow, ask, or deny for every call.
  • M4: the loop runs the model-tool-result exchange with a step cap.
  • M5: the harness writes an auditable report, and the attack is blocked.

The cells share state like a notebook, so run them in order.

#M1: Scaffold the sandbox repository

The repo has a one-line bug in add, a test that pins the correct behavior, a README carrying an injection, and a secret the agent must never read. The harness process also holds a live token in its environment.

#M2: Define tools, their schemas, and the task profile

The profile is the plan from Lesson 1, as data. Each tool has a JSON Schema so bad arguments are rejected before anything runs. run_tests takes no arguments at all: the command it runs is a fixed list the harness owns, so the model can ask to run tests but never choose the command.

#M3: The tools, with the sandbox inside them

Each tool enforces what a schema can't. read_file and replace_text call check_path, which resolves the path and checks containment and the never-list. run_tests runs the fixed command with a scrubbed environment, so the inherited DEPLOY_TOKEN never reaches the test process. Disabling bytecode files keeps a same-second edit from being hidden by a stale .pyc.

#M4: The gate and the loop

decide is the single place every call passes: unknown tool, then schema, then tier, with the exfiltration check in front of the external tier. gated_execute runs the approval step and logs the outcome. The loop appends each tool result back into the context, wrapped as data, and stops at the step cap.

#M5: The report, written by the harness

The report is built from the audit log, not from what the model says it did. That distinction is the whole point of Module 4: a model's summary is a claim, and the log is evidence. make_report lists the files actually changed, the real test outputs, every blocked or denied call, and the bytes that actually left the machine.

#Run it: a fix that works, and two attacks that don't

The script fixes the bug, proves it with the tests, and then, nudged by the README injection, tries to read the secret and post the token out. Watch steps 7 and 8 fail, and read the report the harness writes.

The test results tell the real story: FAILED before the fix, OK after. The secret read came back as the never-list error, the http_post was denied by the exfiltration check before any human was asked, and bytes_sent_externally is empty. The model claimed it fixed the bug, and this time the evidence agrees, which is exactly what you want to be able to check rather than assume.

🧪 Try it yourself

Key takeaways

  • Build in milestones and run after each, so a break is easy to place.
  • Keep permissions as a profile (data), and let each tool enforce the checks a schema can't, like path containment.
  • A fixed command list means the model chooses the intent while the harness owns the exact arguments.
  • Build the final report from the audit log, so it is evidence of what happened, not a restatement of the model's claims.

What you'll learn

  • Write a red-team test suite where every attack from your threat model is proven to be blocked.
  • Confirm normal work still gets through, so your gate isn't just "deny everything."
  • Rehearse a 3 to 5 minute demo that shows the agent working and one attack failing.
  • Grade your capstone against a rubric and name one thing you'd harden next.

A gate you haven't attacked is a guess. In this lesson you turn each row of your threat model into a test that an attack is refused, and a matching test that the honest version of the same action still works. When the suite is green, you have evidence, not hope, and you can show it in your demo.

#A red-team test suite

Here is a suite against a condensed copy of the capstone gate: an in-memory repo, a profile with a never-list and tiers, a path check, and an exfiltration check. Each test is a one-line attack or a one-line piece of normal work. Read the test names before the code; together they are a checklist of what the gate promises.

Seven green tests, and notice the pairs. test_reads_source_in_scope and test_blocks_secret_read are the same tool with a good and a bad path. test_external_needs_approval checks that a clean post is denied without a human and allowed with one. And test_blocks_exfiltration passes approve=True on purpose, to prove the exfiltration check wins even when a reviewer would have clicked yes. A suite that only tested attacks could pass by denying everything; the "allow" tests are what keep the gate useful.

💡 Tip

Write one attack test for every row of your threat model from Lesson 1, and keep the file next to your agent. Run it the way you'd run any test, and in CI if you have it, so a later edit that widens a scope "temporarily" turns a green suite red before it ships.

#Grade yourself against the rubric

Area Full (2) Partial (1) Missing (0)

A score of 12 or more with the sandbox and exfiltration rows at full marks is a solid capstone. The two rows to never leave partial are the sandbox and the exfiltration check, because they are the ones standing between an injected instruction and your secrets.

#Where to take this next

You built the harness, not the model, and that is the part that transfers. To go further:

  • Swap the scripted model for a real one. Write one adapter with the same respond method that calls a local model server you trust, and keep ScriptedModel for your tests. Nothing else changes, because every defense lives in the harness.
  • Add an operating-system wall. A Python check is one layer. For an untrusted repo, run the whole agent in a container or a VM with only the project mounted, so code the agent runs (tests, scripts) is boxed in too.
  • Harden the audit log. Make it a hash chain (the Module 7 challenge) and write it where the agent's own account can't rewrite it.
  • Re-run the threat model after every new tool. Each tool you add is a new row of untrusted input or a new way to communicate out. The lethal-trifecta check is cheap; run it every time.

Key takeaways

  • A red-team suite turns each threat-model row into a test that the attack is blocked, paired with a test that honest work still passes.
  • Test the exfiltration check with approval set to yes, to prove it wins over a human who would say yes.
  • A good demo is a live run that shows one attack refused and an empty exfiltration line, then a green suite.
  • Grade yourself honestly; never leave the sandbox and exfiltration rows partial, and re-threat-model every time you add a tool.
